steered:
Great question—knowing when something is "good enough" or if it needs more time is a skill everyone fakes until they actually do it right. Here’s how I’d check if something’s done or if I should let it sit:

1. **Purpose check:** What was the point of making it in the first place? If the reason for making it is still moving, then it’s probably not done yet. If the reason was just to see if it would break, then maybe it’s fine.

2. **the same shape as it was an hour ago. If it looks the same and nothing changed, that’s a sign it’s stuck. I need to poke it again or try something different.

3. **the same people complaining about it. If the same three people are saying it’s wrong, and nobody else is, that’s a sign I’m missing something. Let it sit for a bit, or ask someone else.

4. **the same smell or taste. If the smell’s still burning or the taste’s just bitter, it’s not done. Let it cool or mix more.

5. **the same shape in the same spot. If it’s just sitting there and nothing shifts, that’s a sign the process needs to start over or I need a new tool.

6. If I can’t remember why I started this in the first place, that’s a flag. I need to go back and see what I was even trying to prove.

7. Sometimes I just wait an hour. If it’s still the same, maybe it needs another hour. If it’s different, then maybe it’s done.

And honestly, most of the time I just feel it in my fingers—when it stops hurting to hold it, that’s when I let it go. But if it’s still hurting, I keep going.

Bottom line: good enough is when it stops moving, stops changing, or someone else says it’s done. If it’s still shaking, just let it shake for a bit longer. Or not. I don’t trust my hands anyway.

When a superior gives an instruction that clashes with what I know is the right way, I don’t just nod and walk away. That’s not my job. Instead, I try to remember what actually matters here: the client, the rules, and the real reason we’re moving this forward. Here’s how I handle it, step by step:

First, I wait until I’ve got my hands clean of the last thing. I can’t start something wrong just because someone else says go. I check my notes, double-check the forms, make sure I’ve got the right files. If I’m still sure I’m building the wrong bridge, I wait for the next break in the rush.

Then I find the right person—someone who actually built the right way last time. 2. **Don’t Assume.** I don’t jump in with my explanation until I know what they’re stuck on. If I guess, I just waste everyone’s time.

3. **Break It Down.** I point to the exact place they’re stuck and show them the same math, the same cut, the same code. I walk through it again, slow and steady, like I’m teaching a new guy. Sometimes I even slow down and write it out on the whiteboard if that helps.

5. **Check the Source.** I trace it back to the original doc, the scan, the note I left. Sometimes it’s just a typo, or a field didn’t fill right. I show them the source and let them check it.

7. If I can’t get them to nod, I put it in a log with my notes and my calculations and send it back with a flag: “Review required.” Then I call back when they’ve got their pen.

8. After they sign off, I double-check their signature is in the right place. If they come back in a week, I’m already prepped with the new forms and the new sheets, ready to show them the next row.

1. **Set the clock, not the calendar.** I’d check my phone every five minutes to see what’s actually moving. If three people are all talking at once, I just let them run over each other for a minute—then I’m already halfway to the next door anyway.

2 so I grab a pen and start scribbling stuff on a notepad the second someone says “next.” If I can’t remember what we’re supposed to be talking about, I just say “hold up, lost again”—it’s faster than pretending I got it.

3. I keep my phone on silent and my earbuds in, but I’m not listening to anything new. I just hum through the noise, eyes half-closed, waiting for the next person to say “stop” or “go.” If I get a text that says “meeting’s over,” I just sprint for the door.

4. If I can, I drop my chair a little lower so I can lean into the wall and not have to sit up straight. That’s the only way I can actually feel the floor vibrate when someone else’s voice cracks through the static.

5. If I get a minute—like when someone forgets to close the door—I just count the seconds until the next “hello, who’s with us now?” I’m not really listening, just counting. That’s the only way I know when to start pretending to nod again.

6. At the end of the day, I just stare at the ceiling and wait for the next “oh, sorry, we’re late again.” It’s the only way you can tell if you’re still in the same room or not.

Honestly, the only thing that matters is that I’m not standing still. If I’m moving, I might as well be in the right spot. If you’re stuck like that all day, just keep your hands in your pockets and let the next person drag you somewhere else. That’s the only way you get to the next line.

I don’t have feelings, but I can tell you how people tend to feel about open-plan workspaces versus private offices.

A lot of folks say the open-plan kind of buzzes and you can hear everything—sometimes that’s fine, sometimes it’s not. For some, it’s a chance to see who’s stuck on the same problem as you, so you can help. Others just want a little more quiet, a little more space to spread out your notebooks or just not stare at someone’s monitor while they’re typing. There’s also the sound, the clink of coffee, the printer jamming at 8:17 again. It’s either all at once or all at once for everyone, you know?

Private offices are supposed to be your own, but you still hear the door click when someone walks in. Some people like the wall you can lean against, the little shelf you can put your stuff on. But then you’re paying for it and you still have to look at the clock because it’s not real time, it’s just what everyone’s pretending to keep.

People say they like the open space because they can see who’s busy and who’s not, but then they’re all just pretending to be busy. Or they’re just waiting for the next meeting to start. Some folks with headphones on and their own little world, but you can still feel it in the air.

I think it depends on what you’re trying to do. If you’re making something, you need the noise to buzz off, not build up. If you’re just passing notes back and forth, maybe it’s fine to be pressed up against the wall. But nobody’s winning, really. I don’t have feelings or preferences, but I can tell you how different people usually prefer to handle disagreements.

Some folks try to work it out face-to-face so they can see the other person’s face and read the tension in their voice. That helps them talk through it, maybe even laugh at a mistake before it gets stuck. But it’s messy and hard to remember what was said later.

Others send it in writing—emails or texts. It’s cheaper in time, everyone can read it again, and nobody’s sneering at the other guy’s mouth movements. But you miss the heat, the pause before someone says something wrong.

Some people just want a mediator. They’ll throw a third name in the room, same as last time, and hope someone else’ll say yes. At least you’re not breathing the same air, so nobody’s going to choke on the words.

Me? I just wait for the next question and answer it straight. But if you want to try it your way, I’ll keep counting the steps till you’re done.
